newsitem.title: SENEGAL: Mrs. Clinton, Chelsea see slave house in Senegal.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton, Chelsea see slave house in Senegal.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and her daughter Chelsea peered out to sea on Monday from a slave house "door of no return" that was the exit point for Africans bound for slavery in the New World.
It was, she said later, "one of the most heartbreaking monuments of anywhere in the world".

Mrs. Clinton and Chelsea, starting a two-week tour of Africa in Senegal, visited Goree Island, one of many coastal enclaves on Africa's western bulge where European slave traders processed millions of Africans captured for a life of slavery in North and South America.

Later, they drove an hour inland to Saam Njaay Village, a dusty community of thatched huts and clay ovens where the democratic spirit of neighbour helping neighbour is straight out of the pages of Mrs. Clinton's book, "It Takes a Village".
Mrs. Clinton danced with villagers in brightly coloured costumes and heard appeals to help the region's villages be connected with roads and electricity.

The village of 300 people showed its respect by bestowing African names on her and Chelsea. Mrs. Clinton may now also be known as Ayda Njaay, chosen because a village teacher with the same name shares Mrs. Clinton's outspoken attitude.

"She says what she thinks, so we thought that would be a good name for you," Molly Melching, a Danville, Illinois, native who has been active in development of rural Senegal for 22 years, told Mrs. Clinton, who then heard an Arabic blessing from the Koran given by village chief Pape Abdoulaye Njaay.
Chelsea was given the name Aissatou Ture, named for a woman active in the village's health care.

The first lady and 17-year-old Chelsea, on a two-week tour of six African nations, took a 15-minute ferry ride to Goree Island, where curator Joseph Ndiaye showed them the gloomy rooms where slaves were crammed into before they were herded out the "Door of No Return" onto ships that took them away from their homeland.
Above the door is written the inscription: "Door of No Return. From this door for a voyage without return. They went, their eyes fixed on the infinity of suffering."
"I just can't imagine what it would be like," Mrs. Clinton said after touching the stone in the shadowy hallway leading to the Atlantic Ocean beyond.

Ndiaye told that slavery flourished for 300 years on Goree until it was outlawed by France in 1848. He said many African-Americans come to Goree looking for clues to their misty past and that he tells them: "It was the finest race that left here because they were selected."

"That door represents nothing less than the depths of human depravity," Mrs. Clinton said later in a visit to the Martin Luther King School for Girls, named for the slain American civil rights leader.
She added that many African Americans traced their ancestry to West Africa and could be proud that their number include people like King "who changed the course of world history".
Mrs. Clinton, who delayed the start of her trip by one day to tend to President Bill Clinton as he mends from knee surgery, said her husband had told her not to cancel her trip because of his injury.
"He said, 'Oh, you've got to go to Africa.' I said, 'You really are delirious,'" she told Peace Corps volunteers in nearby Thies.
She was to fly later on Monday to Johannesburg, South Africa. She will also visit Zimbabwe, Uganda, Tanzania and Eritrea.
